title: The last freedom
hook: Frankl: the freedom to choose one's attitude can't be taken (Man's Search for Meaning)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Frankl and the grieving doctor, and a question that gave a loss its meaning. Your line was meaning, even here. Who was your hard task for? Today, a piece of bread in the evening. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Evening, in a prisoners' hut. Everyone is starving. The daily ration is a little bread and thin soup, and every crumb counts. And Frankl remembers men who walked through the huts comforting others, and giving away their last piece of bread. He says there may have been few of them. But they were there. And for him, that was proof of something. Not about how strong they were. About what can and can't be taken from a person. Today: the last freedom.
screen: `EVENING IN A PRISONERS' HUT.` → `MEN WHO GAVE AWAY THEIR LAST BREAD.` → `WHAT CAN'T BE TAKEN?`

segments.voice: First, what was taken. Frankl's account of the camps is a list of losses: his name replaced by a number, his clothes, his hair, his manuscript, and no knowledge of whether the people he loved were alive. Everything a person usually leans on, gone. Second, what wasn't. Out of watching those men in the huts, Frankl draws his conclusion, in paraphrase: everything can be taken from a person but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances, to choose one's own way. Third, how small it can be. In his account, this freedom isn't a grand speech. It's a shared crust. A kind word to the man in the next bunk. Once, marching in the cold, Frankl kept himself going by picturing himself in a warm lecture hall, describing the camp as something to be studied. That was his own way: turning toward the suffering as something to understand, not only something to endure. Fourth, what it isn't. This is not a grade for anyone in pain. Frankl writes as a witness, not a judge, and the freedom he describes is a door that's there, not a test some people fail. And it doesn't excuse anyone who causes suffering. The camps were a crime; the freedom he found inside them doesn't make them less of one. It just means that even there, one small choice was still a person's own: the stance they took toward what was happening.
screen: `WHAT WAS TAKEN: ALMOST EVERYTHING.` · `WHAT WASN'T: HOW TO MEET IT.` · `A CRUST. A KIND WORD. A LECTURE HALL.` · `A DOOR, NOT A GRADE.` · then, large: `THE LAST FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one small thing from today that happened without asking you: a changed schedule, a person's mood, a late bus, an ache. Let it be there. Then notice there's still a small space between it and you: the space where you decide how to meet it. You don't have to fill that space with anything big. Try a few words for it: patient, curious, kind, honest, steady. See which one fits today. Let it settle into the body. The bell holds the time.
The last freedom. Frankl's phrase for what couldn't be taken, even in the camps: choosing how to meet what's happening. Today's word.
Your line: my attitude. Today, when something happens that you didn't choose, take one breath and pick the word you'll meet it with. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Frankl, and some counselors trained in his logotherapy, practice noticing the space between what happens and how they respond, and choosing a stance toward what they can't change.

fork.setup: you're Frankl, marching in the freezing cold, exhausted. what keeps you going?
options: picturing yourself lecturing about the camp in a warm hall.
counting the steps until the end.
fork.reveal: he pictures himself in a lecture hall, studying the suffering instead of only enduring it. his own way of meeting it.

trapdoor: what you thought: think positive and you'll be fine.
what it means: when almost everything is taken, a person can still choose the stance they take toward it, in small acts like a shared crust.
what a scholar hears: Man's Search for Meaning, part one: the last of the human freedoms, drawn from the men in the huts, and the root of the attitudinal values in Frankl's logotherapy.

notes: Frankl is in copyright; everything is paraphrased, including the phrase the last of the human freedoms (left unquoted).

Part one paraphrased: the men who walked through the huts comforting others and giving away their last piece of bread, 'they may have been few in number'; 'everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms...'. Confirm.
Losses listed: number for a name, clothes, shaved hair, the manuscript he carried, no news of family. Confirm each against part one. 'His work' (as a doctor) is a loose summary; cut if not supported.
Lecture-hall image: on a march Frankl imagines himself lecturing on the psychology of the concentration camp in a warm, well-lit room; confirm.
'A door, not a grade' and 'the camps were a crime' are the script's framing, added so the day never blames people who suffered. Confirm tone.
Editor: cut the loosely supported 'his work' from the list of losses; reworded the practice prompt so it doesn't repeat day 727's 'one thing you can't change' or day 728's weather.
